headline: E-commerce fulfilment is rewriting what a Saudi warehouse has to do
deck: A building designed to ship pallets and one designed to ship parcels are different buildings, and the second is more expensive per square metre.
excerpt: E-commerce fulfilment and last-mile delivery are declared segments at the Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo. Both impose requirements that a conventional distribution warehouse was never designed to meet, and both are what make automation economics work.
content:
E-commerce fulfilment and last-mile delivery sit among the declared segments at the Saudi Warehousing & Logistics Expo in Riyadh, and between them they explain why the automation content on that floor exists.

A conventional distribution warehouse ships pallets. Goods arrive by the pallet, are stored by the pallet, are picked by the pallet or the case, and leave on a lorry to a shop or another warehouse. The building is a volume with racking in it, the handling equipment is forklifts, and the labour requirement is modest relative to the throughput.

A fulfilment centre ships parcels. Goods arrive by the pallet and leave as individual items in thousands of small orders a day, each of which has to be located, picked, packed, labelled, sorted by destination and handed to a courier within a promised window.

Almost every physical characteristic of the building changes as a result. Storage has to be organised for fast retrieval of single items rather than dense stacking of pallets. Aisle layouts change. Packing stations, sortation equipment and outbound dispatch dominate floor area that a distribution warehouse would give to racking. The labour requirement per unit of throughput rises by an order of magnitude, and it concentrates in picking, which is the most repetitive task in the building.

That last point is where automation stops being an efficiency and becomes a precondition. Goods-to-person systems, shuttle storage and sortation exist because picking single items by walking to them does not scale past a certain order volume at any acceptable cost.

The Saudi relevance is straightforward. E-commerce volumes in the Kingdom have grown into the range where dedicated fulfilment operations are justified, and the exhibitor list at the show pairs national logistics operators with the European materials handling manufacturers — Swisslog, SSI Schäfer, Kardex — whose equipment addresses exactly this problem.

Last mile is the other half and it is a different engineering problem again. Delivery density determines cost per parcel, and density in Saudi cities varies enormously between dense urban districts and low-density suburban development. Route planning, parcel lockers, pickup points and vehicle selection are all responses to that variation.

The property consequence is where the two meet. Fulfilment centres want to be near consumption to shorten the last mile, which puts them on more expensive land closer to cities, which in turn strengthens the case for building upward and denser — and therefore for automation. Land price, labour cost and order profile all push the same way once parcels rather than pallets are the unit.

The expo runs from 8 to 10 September at the Riyadh International Convention & Exhibition Center.
